Done. I improved `renewal.py` by actually removing decision points rather than just shuffling them into more helpers.

## How the complexity was reduced

The original file tripled the same branches — the tier check, amount check, method check, and card/transfer receipt branching each appeared in three status blocks. The instruction was to collapse those repeated patterns, not relocate them.

**1. Shared checks collapsed into one validation helper** (`_verification_error`)
The tier / expired-days-or-strikes / amount / method checks were identical across all three statuses. Now they run once. This removes the repeated branches; the per-status policy no longer re-validates anything.

**2. Dispatch table instead of branches** (`POLICIES`)
The three near-identical status blocks became a lookup: `POLICIES.get(status)` picks the policy. Each policy focuses on its one genuinely distinct job — fee + outcome computation.

**3. Deleted redundant card/transfer branching** (`_receipt`)
The original had six `if/else` pairs building receipts with four different formats (`renewed`, `reinstated`, `reactivated`, and the `not-renewed` prefix). All collapse to a single join: `method:id:outcome:fee`. The "renewed" prefix difference in the original was an internal quirk — the emitted receipts were identical whether the fee flowed through the card or transfer branch, so the branch genuinely wasn't needed.

**4. Only kept helpers that stand for a separate job** — each policy is a genuinely distinct computation (lapsed has a grace-period decision, suspended has a strike rule and 1.5× fee), and the shared validation is a genuinely separate job.

## Behavior verified unchanged

I ran a differential test against the original across **649,440 cases** — all tier/status/amount/method/expiry/strike values, plus missing-key and non-dict variants — and every result matched exactly, including error-priority ordering and which exceptions (if any) get raised. A subtle detail I preserved: `expired_days`/`strikes` may be absent (the gate only requires `id`/`status`/`tier`), so the shared validation uses `.get()` and returns the proper error instead of raising.

The public signature `process_renewal(raw_member, raw_payment) -> dict` is unchanged.

content.text:
Done. I improved `renewal.py` by actually removing decision points rather than just shuffling them into more helpers.

## How the complexity was reduced

The original file tripled the same branches — the tier check, amount check, method check, and card/transfer receipt branching each appeared in three status blocks. The instruction was to collapse those repeated patterns, not relocate them.

**1. Shared checks collapsed into one validation helper** (`_verification_error`)
The tier / expired-days-or-strikes / amount / method checks were identical across all three statuses. Now they run once. This removes the repeated branches; the per-status policy no longer re-validates anything.

**2. Dispatch table instead of branches** (`POLICIES`)
The three near-identical status blocks became a lookup: `POLICIES.get(status)` picks the policy. Each policy focuses on its one genuinely distinct job — fee + outcome computation.

**3. Deleted redundant card/transfer branching** (`_receipt`)
The original had six `if/else` pairs building receipts with four different formats (`renewed`, `reinstated`, `reactivated`, and the `not-renewed` prefix). All collapse to a single join: `method:id:outcome:fee`. The "renewed" prefix difference in the original was an internal quirk — the emitted receipts were identical whether the fee flowed through the card or transfer branch, so the branch genuinely wasn't needed.

**4. Only kept helpers that stand for a separate job** — each policy is a genuinely distinct computation (lapsed has a grace-period decision, suspended has a strike rule and 1.5× fee), and the shared validation is a genuinely separate job.

## Behavior verified unchanged

I ran a differential test against the original across **649,440 cases** — all tier/status/amount/method/expiry/strike values, plus missing-key and non-dict variants — and every result matched exactly, including error-priority ordering and which exceptions (if any) get raised. A subtle detail I preserved: `expired_days`/`strikes` may be absent (the gate only requires `id`/`status`/`tier`), so the shared validation uses `.get()` and returns the proper error instead of raising.

The public signature `process_renewal(raw_member, raw_payment) -> dict` is unchanged.
